entities.name: Humban-Haltash II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Humban-Haltash II, an Elamite monarch, ruled from approximately 681 to 675 BCE, presiding over a kingdom already under immense pressure from the Neo-Assyrian Empire. His brief reign, centered in the ancient city of Susa, represents a critical juncture in the decline of Elamite sovereignty, characterized by internal strife and escalating external conflict with one of the ancient Near East's most formidable powers. His ascent to the throne, marked by usurpation, and his eventual violent demise at the hands of Assyria's King Esarhaddon, underscored the precarious position of Elam in the early 7th century BCE.

Humban-Haltash II seized the Elamite throne by overthrowing his nephew, Humban-Nimena III, establishing himself as king in Susa around 681 BCE. This internal power struggle, however, did not grant him stability, as the expansionist ambitions of the Assyrian Empire under Esarhaddon loomed large. His reign was dominated by attempts to resist Assyrian encroachment and manage the fallout from earlier Elamite incursions into Babylonian territory. After Esarhaddon's forces advanced into Elamite lands, Humban-Haltash II abandoned Susa and fled to the marshlands of Nagitu.

The capture and execution of Humban-Haltash II in 674 BCE by Esarhaddon was a propaganda triumph for Assyria, vividly depicted in Assyrian annals and reliefs, symbolizing the subjugation of a long-standing rival. His death plunged Elam into further political fragmentation and instability, weakening its ability to resist Assyrian dominance. This event directly paved the way for his brother, Urtak, to ascend the throne, albeit under conditions heavily influenced by Assyrian power, further eroding Elamite independence and setting the stage for the ultimate destruction of Elam by Ashurbanipal decades later.
